analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal office to publicly manufacture insulin, inhalers, naloxone, EpiPens, and antibiotics at fair prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral in the House and received no vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services. The office would make drugs itself or contract with nonprofits and public partners, set a fair price, and prioritize medicines where patients face high prices, shortages, or few makers. It specifically required public manufacturing of every major type of insulin, at least one asthma/COPD inhaler, an epinephrine auto-injector, naloxone, and at least three antibiotics within a year. It would also bar former drug-industry lobbyists from running or working in the office.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay high prices for insulin, inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors, and naloxone; people who depend on drugs with chronic shortages or few manufacturers; and federal and state health programs like Medicare, Medicaid, VA, and defense health systems, which the office would be required to buy from at fair prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients on insulin, inhalers, and allergy drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the new Office of Drug Manufacturing to begin public manufacturing, within one year of enactment, of at least one insulin product of each dosage form and each type of insulin, one asthma/COPD inhaler, an epinephrine auto-injector, naloxone for community use, and at least three antibiotics. [S2]

The office would set a fair price for each drug considering patient access, the cost to federal and state health programs, and manufacturing cost, and all prices would be made publicly available. [S2]

The office would target 'applicable drugs' that are no longer or barely competitive — drugs with only three or fewer manufacturers that have raised prices above inflation, are on the FDA shortage list, or are essential medicines priced beyond patient access. [S2]
Former registered drug-industry lobbyists and senior executives of drug companies under federal enforcement actions would be barred from directing or working at the office for six years. [S2]

Sales proceeds would fund the office's activities, and if a buyer of an approved application raised prices above the fair price or failed to market the drug, the office would revoke the application and resume production. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name and generic drug makers that profit from drugs with few competitors and from persistently high prices, plus taxpayers to the extent the office's startup costs exceed its sales revenue, since the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' with no dedicated funding source.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers; taxpayers for startup costs

drawbacks.text: The bill contains no dedicated funding stream — it authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' from general appropriations, so the program's startup costs would fall on taxpayers until sales revenue covers them. [S2]

It would put the federal government in direct competition with private generic manufacturers, raising the practical challenge of running FDA-approved pharmaceutical plants at commercial quality and scale, and it allows contracting with private entities only with a stated preference for nonprofits and public partners. [S2]

Mandated purchase minimums for VA, Defense, Public Health Service, and Coast Guard buyers would channel federal demand toward the office's products, and a buyer losing money on an overpriced private alternative has no equivalent recourse under the bill. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing four-figure insulin and EpiPen costs and recurring shortages of essential medicines, the upside is direct and large: a public manufacturer would both sell at fair prices and force existing makers to compete. The costs are real but ordinary for a new public enterprise — an open-ended appropriation, manufacturing risk, and disruption to incumbent generic makers — and the bill's safeguards (FDA review without special deference, price transparency, revocation of misused applications) are designed to limit them. The main honest objection is not the design but the political difficulty of sustaining funding for a government drug company against an industry that profits from the status quo.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on December 5, 2023, by Rep. Jan Schakowsky. [S1]
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on December 5, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Health on December 8, 2023. [S4]
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — is recorded in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 118th Congress. [S4]
The bill's 10 cosponsors were all House Democrats. [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers whose profits rest on drugs with few competitors and high prices — particularly makers of insulin, inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors, and naloxone — were better off because the bill never moved, as were their allied distributors and middlemen. No company had to compete with a public manufacturer or justify its prices against a public benchmark.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 5, 2023, and sponsored it in the House. [S1]

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and never took it up for a hearing or markup. [S4]

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup, leaving it stalled in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats, the sole sponsor was a Democrat, and a Republican committee chair controlled whether it advanced; no Republican supported the bill in the record. [S3][S4]

industries.note: The office would target drugs with three or fewer manufacturers and above-inflation price hikes — the business model of high-price, low-competition brand-name products — and would sell insulin, inhalers, epinephrine auto-injectors, and naloxone at fair prices, directly undercutting incumbents' pricing power. Insulin makers, inhaler makers, and EpiPen's maker would face a public competitor for the first time. [S2]

Some generic makers would lose sales where a public manufacturer enters their markets, but the office's ability to manufacture active pharmaceutical ingredients that are in short supply would lower input costs and make market entry easier for many of the same companies. [S2]

industries.industry: Drug wholesalers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: They would be required participants on the office's advisory council and remain the distribution channel for publicly manufactured drugs, but transparent public pricing would weaken the opaque markup and rebate structures through which they earn revenue. [S2]

Former registered drug-industry lobbyists would be barred from directing or working in the new office for six years, and executives of companies under federal enforcement would likewise be excluded — reducing the industry's influence over a new part of the drug supply. [S2]
